description: Classic pop/rock hit progression (Axis progression). Extremely common in modern rock and pop; strong, catchy, and easy to sing over.
Traditional rock cadence (tonic–subdominant–dominant). Ubiquitous in early rock’n’roll and classic rock.
Rotation of the Axis progression starting on vi. Very common in modern pop-rock and EDM; feels emotional but still uplifting.
Grunge/punk feel with a Mixolydian flavor. Staple of classic rock and punk riffs.
Metal/industrial, dark modal motion with a descending bass line. Great for heavy, looping riffs.
American-style pop-punk, slightly softer than I–IV–V. Works well for fast, driving songs.
Modal interchange with bIII and bVI gives alternative/cinematic color. Good for 90s alt-rock and soundtrack vibes.
Punk rock drive with a Mixolydian touch. Great for energetic choruses and gang vocals.
Extended 50s-style progression with a vintage vibe. Good for doo-wop, retro rock or playful bridges.
Phrygian-ish tension with a half-step clash. Very common in heavy metal and industrial riffs.
Heavy metal feel with dense chromatic motion. Great for stomping mid-tempo riffs.
Power-metal classic with a heroic/epic sound. Perfect for big choruses and guitar harmonies.
Chromatic diminished passing chord into the dominant. Good for neoclassical metal and dramatic builds.
Unusual major progression with modal color (iii as a lift, bVII as rock flavor). Fits alternative and progressive rock.
Metallic loop with a strong sense of journey and return. Great for power-metal choruses and melodic metalcore hooks.
Core jazz cadence. Appears in thousands of standards; good for turnarounds and reharmonizations.
Jazz turnaround. Standard end-of-phrase pattern in jazz and sophisticated pop.
Extended dominant cycle. Useful for intros, interludes and modulating sections.
Long jazz/classic chain with smooth resolution. Great template for lush ballads.
European-style classical cadence with inversions. Typical of late-Romantic tonal harmony.
Rock suspense: sus4 delaying the 3rd before resolving to V–I. Classic stadium-rock gesture.
Light, airy feel with IVsus2 resolving to IV. Fits clean-guitar textures, indie and post-rock.
V in first inversion for a smoother bass line. Good for subtle, polished pop-rock harmony.
Chromatic diminished color plus ii–V–I resolution. Nice for bridges and modulations.
Atmospheric add9 chords with open, lush sound. Great for post-rock, electro-rock and modern worship.
Natural minor, classic for metal/goth/industrial. Strong, simple loop for riffs and choruses.
Descending minor motion; feels epic and ‘northern’. Fits folk/pagan/Viking metal and big rock themes.
Natural-minor counterpart of I–IV–V. Staple minor-key rock and punk loop.
Harmonic-minor variant with major V. Strong drama and pull back to i; common in metal.
Cinematic natural-minor chain i–VI–III–VII. Very emotional; often used in intros, verses and big choruses.
Rising minor cycle with growing tension. Great for build-ups and pre-choruses.
Phrygian minor: i–bII–i. Extremely dark and exotic; classic in extreme metal.
Cyclic natural-minor motion. Good for verses that feel stuck or obsessive.
Power-metal minor with heroic feel. Great for big, soaring choruses.
Thrash/industrial chromatic chain. Feels mechanical and relentless.
Thick, gloomy loop with no full resolution. Good for doom/sludge and darker alt-rock.
Extended Phrygian minor loop. Very tense and exotic; fits progressive/extreme metal.
Modal minor with IV and VII. Excellent for alternative rock/metal and dynamic verse/chorus contrasts.
Post-rock / post-metal style long arc. Feels like a journey through different levels of tension.
Minor classical/jazz cadence. Basic ii°–V–i pattern for minor-key resolutions.
Jazz ii–V–i in minor with altered dominant. Very expressive in dark ballads.
Extended minor chain with classical flavor. Good for intros and codas in film/score writing.
Full classical-style minor progression. Long journey through functional harmony back to tonic.
Suspense progression in minor: sus4 delays the resolution. Good for dramatic refrains in metal and dark rock.
Atmospheric minor with lush add9 color. Fits industrial, cinematic and ambient electronica.
Inversions for smoother bass in minor. Works for introspective rock and metal ballads.
Modern minor sound mixing sus2 with modal VII. Good for post-rock and ambient metal builds.
Experimental chromatic move around IV using #iv°. Nice for quirky modulations and art-rock transitions.
Half–whole diminished-type color; very tense and unstable. Good for horror cues and experimental metal.
Alt/rock chromatic chain with dim7 tension. Fits progressive, math-rock and artsy intros/bridges.
Almost resolves through bV then snaps back to i. Unsettling, ‘broken resolution’ effect.
Strong chromatic shifts around the tonic. Works for psychedelic rock and avant-garde sections.
Natural-minor loop with a flat, numb feel. Famous from Nirvana-style grunge (Fm: Fm–Bbm–Ab–Db); quintessential 90s chord color.
Epic minor progression widely used in rock and pop ballads. Very emotional, often heard in big, cinematic verses and choruses.
Descending minor loop i–VII–VI–iv with anthem-like quality. Great for choruses that should feel both heavy and singable.
Minor tonic to bright III major then rock VII back to i. Classic 90s alt-rock color.
Minor equivalent of a big pop ballad: i–VI–iv–V. Great for emotional rock/metal choruses.
Minor with VI and VII leading to III. Cinematic sound; perfect for post-rock and metal instrumentals.
Natural-minor verse loop; introspective but forward-moving. Good for verses that open into brighter choruses.
i–iv–vi°–V: minor with diminished vi pulling strongly to V. Suitable for gothic rock and darker jazz-influenced sections.
Classic 50s-style progression I–vi–IV–V. Used in countless oldies and nostalgic rock ballads.
Axis-family variant with ii instead of vi. A bit brighter; works for modern pop-rock.
Major I–III–IV then iv modal mixture. Good for bittersweet choruses that start happy but end with a minor twist.
Very common rock/proto-punk loop. Strong driving pattern for verses and choruses.
Simple folk/rock movement. Great for roots rock, Americana and straightforward choruses.
Mixin’ rock staple: I–bVII–IV–I. Very typical for Southern rock and guitar-driven anthems.
Blues/rock color with bIII and bVII. Great for AC/DC-style riffs and classic hard-rock choruses.
Pop-jazz turnaround: I–vi–ii–V. Common in standards and jazz-influenced pop/rock.
Axis-like but landing on ii for a slightly unresolved feel. Good for bridges and pre-choruses.
Chromatic descending minor riff i–bVII–bVI–bV. Great for thrash and industrial guitar lines.
Chromatic climb from i to bVI. Fits extreme metal and industrial when used as power-chords.
i–v–bVI–bVII: classic metal movement with v minor. Good for driving verses.
Epic loop where VI and VII both lean back into i. Great for heroic riffs and metal themes.
Minor with rock-style IV borrowed from relative major. Feels like a minor take on classic I–bVII–IV rock.
Descending rock pattern in minor. Works in doom/stoner contexts when slowed down and fuzzed.
Minor to IV then drop to bVII. Fits grunge and alternative mid-tempo choruses.
Mix of natural VI and Phrygian bII. Very dark; good for extreme industrial/blackened textures.
I–bVII–bIII–IV: high-energy punk/alt-rock color. Great for power-chord riffs with shouted vocals.
Mixolydian-blues hybrid. Good for hardcore breakdowns and mid-tempo punk choruses.
Tight descending minor loop; simple and brutal. Perfect for fast punk or hardcore in minor keys.
Minor take on Oi!/street-punk style progression. Good for chant-style choruses.
1–5–4–6 progression, close relative of the Axis pattern. Works well in modern pop/EDM and as a twist on I–V–vi–IV.
Classic EDM minor loop i–VI–VII–i. Great for progressive house and trance drops with emotional hooks.
VI–VII–v–i–VII: descending-bass minor pattern. Good for rolling basslines in D&B and techno.
Minor EDM tool: i–v–VI–VII. Feels more driving and less pop than i–VI–VII–i.
Emotional minor loop with IV and III. Good for liquid D&B, future garage and melancholic electronica.
Starts on iv for an ‘in the middle of the story’ feeling. Useful for mid-section loops in D&B and breaks.
House-friendly major progression: I–V–vi–iii. Good for uplifting house and trance leads.
I–iii–vi–IV adds a bittersweet iii. Fits emotional EDM and French-house-style loops.
Minor progression often used under arpeggiated synth lines. Good for techno-trance hybrids and melodic techno.
Liquid D&B-friendly loop i–VII–III–VI. Strong emotional narrative; great with side-chained pads.
Rotation of Axis chords starting on VI. Typical for modern EDM/pop where the chorus enters on a non-tonic chord.
Minor EDM progression with smooth bass motion. Good for melodic bass music and hybrid trap.
More ‘jazzy’ minor progression useful for lo-fi, IDM and experimental electronica with rich chords.
Emo/alt-rock style loop (e.g. Em–Am–D–C). Strong descending bass feel; great for Midwest emo guitars and post-hardcore verses.
Minor to bright III, then v–IV. Very expressive for melodic hardcore/emo; works well with arpeggiated or ‘twinkly’ guitars.
Axis-family variant often used in pop-punk and emo. Starts on I, dips to vi, then resolves through V–IV; good for choruses that feel both hopeful and sad.
